pn-junction-001.question: How is voltage applied to forward-bias a PN junction diode?
choices: The p side positive and the n side negative
The p side negative and the n side positive
The p side and n side at the same potential
pn-junction-001.explanation: Making the p side (anode) positive and the n side (cathode) negative lowers the potential barrier at the junction, so majority carriers flow across it and a large current flows. This is forward bias. The opposite polarity is reverse bias, under which almost no current flows.

pn-junction-002.question: What happens to the width of the depletion layer when the reverse bias applied to a PN junction is increased?
choices: It narrows
It does not change
It widens
pn-junction-002.explanation: Under reverse bias, the external voltage adds to the built-in potential and pulls carriers further away from the junction, so the depletion layer widens. As it widens, the junction capacitance decreases, a property used in variable-capacitance (varactor) diodes.

pn-junction-003.question: Which phenomenon does a voltage-regulator (Zener) diode mainly use?
choices: Forward diffusion current
Breakdown under reverse bias
Electromotive force from absorbed light
pn-junction-003.explanation: A voltage-regulator diode uses the fact that when the reverse voltage reaches a certain value (the breakdown voltage), current suddenly flows and the voltage stays nearly constant even as the current changes. Breakdown can be Zener breakdown or avalanche breakdown. Electromotive force from light is used in solar cells and photodiodes.

pn-junction-004.question: Which correctly describes the relationship between forward current and forward voltage of a PN junction diode?
choices: Current increases linearly in proportion to voltage
Current increases exponentially with voltage
Current is constant regardless of voltage
pn-junction-004.explanation: Diode current is given by I = Is (exp(qV / nkT) − 1) and increases exponentially with forward voltage. That is why current seems to start flowing suddenly above a certain voltage. Unlike a resistor, voltage and current are not proportional (it does not obey Ohm's law).

pn-junction-005.question: What is the forward voltage (the approximate voltage at which current starts to flow) of a typical silicon PN junction diode?
choices: About 3 V
About 0.1 V
About 0.6–0.7 V
pn-junction-005.explanation: A silicon diode starts conducting significant current when the forward voltage exceeds about 0.6–0.7 V. This value is related to the band gap and varies with material and structure: about 0.2–0.4 V for Schottky barrier diodes and about 3 V for GaN-based blue LEDs.

pn-junction-006.question: How does the reverse saturation current of a PN junction diode depend on temperature?
choices: It increases as temperature rises
It is constant regardless of temperature
It becomes zero as temperature rises
pn-junction-006.explanation: The reverse saturation current is carried by thermally generated minority carriers, so it rises sharply with temperature. In silicon it is said to roughly double for every 10 °C rise. This is one reason leakage current increases at high temperature.

pn-junction-007.question: Which is a characteristic of a Schottky barrier diode?
choices: It is a diode made by joining two p-type semiconductors
It uses a metal-semiconductor junction, with a low forward voltage and fast switching
It emits strong light when forward current flows
pn-junction-007.explanation: A Schottky barrier diode uses a metal-semiconductor junction (Schottky junction). It operates with majority carriers only and has no minority-carrier storage, so its reverse recovery time is short and it is fast. Its forward voltage is also lower than that of a PN junction diode, so it is used in switching power supplies and similar circuits.

pn-junction-008.question: Which property does a variable-capacitance (varactor) diode use?
choices: Emitting light with forward current
Resistance changing with temperature
Junction capacitance changing with reverse bias voltage
pn-junction-008.explanation: When reverse bias is applied to a PN junction, the depletion width changes with voltage and so does the junction capacitance. A varactor diode uses this to control capacitance with voltage. It is used in radio and TV tuners and in voltage-controlled oscillators (VCOs).

pn-junction-009.question: In a PN junction where the p side is far more heavily doped than the n side (a p+n junction), how does the depletion layer spread?
choices: It spreads mostly into the lightly doped n side
It spreads mostly into the heavily doped p side
It always spreads equally into both sides
pn-junction-009.explanation: The amount of ionized impurity charge is equal on both sides of the depletion layer. The lightly doped side must be depleted over a wider region to provide the same charge, so the depletion layer spreads mainly into the lightly doped side. This is a basic idea in designing breakdown voltage.

pn-junction-010.question: Why does a reverse current flow briefly (a reverse recovery time exists) when a PN junction diode is switched from forward to reverse?
choices: Because the metal electrode resistance is large
Because minority carriers stored during forward conduction do not disappear immediately
Because the package heats up
pn-junction-010.explanation: During forward conduction, injected minority carriers are stored on both sides of the junction. After switching to reverse, current flows in the reverse direction until these carriers are swept out or recombine. This time is the reverse recovery time, which causes switching losses and noise.

pn-junction-011.question: How does the built-in (diffusion) potential of a PN junction relate to the doping on each side?
choices: It is constant, independent of doping
It decreases as doping increases
It increases as doping increases
pn-junction-011.explanation: The built-in potential is Vbi = (kT/q) ln(NA × ND / ni²), so it increases with the doping on both sides. For silicon PN junctions it is typically about 0.6–0.9 V.

pn-junction-012.question: Which correctly describes the mechanism of avalanche breakdown?
choices: Carriers accelerated by a high field collide with the lattice and create new electron-hole pairs, which multiply in a chain reaction
Electrons tunnel quantum-mechanically through a thin barrier
The junction melts as the temperature rises
pn-junction-012.explanation: In avalanche breakdown, carriers accelerated by the strong field in the depletion layer collide with atoms and create electron-hole pairs (impact ionization); these are accelerated in turn and collide again, so the current grows like an avalanche. It tends to occur in junctions with relatively low doping and wide depletion layers.

pn-junction-013.question: In a very heavily doped PN junction, what is the main mechanism of breakdown at low reverse voltage?
choices: Avalanche breakdown
Zener breakdown due to quantum-mechanical tunneling
Melting of the junction due to heat
pn-junction-013.explanation: In a junction heavily doped on both sides, the depletion layer is very thin, so electrons in the valence band tunnel through the barrier into the conduction band and current flows. This is Zener breakdown, which occurs at low breakdown voltages of about 5 V or less. At higher breakdown voltages, avalanche breakdown dominates.

pn-junction-014.question: What does a bridge rectifier made of four diodes do?
choices: Converts DC to AC
Amplifies a signal
Full-wave rectifies AC into a current flowing in one direction (pulsating DC)
pn-junction-014.explanation: In a bridge rectifier, a different pair of diodes conducts during the positive and negative half-cycles of the AC, so current flows through the load in the same direction during both half-cycles (full-wave rectification). The output still pulsates, so it is smoothed with a capacitor for use as a DC supply.

pn-junction-015.question: How is a photodiode generally used to detect light?
choices: A large forward current is passed to make it emit light
Reverse bias is applied, and carriers generated by light in the depletion layer are collected as current
AC voltage is applied to make it resonate
pn-junction-015.explanation: Reverse-biasing a photodiode widens the depletion layer; electrons and holes generated there by light are separated by the field, and a current (photocurrent) proportional to light intensity flows. Reverse bias also reduces junction capacitance, giving a faster response.

pn-junction-016.question: How does an LED emit light?
choices: Electrons and holes injected under forward bias emit light when they recombine
It is heated by reverse breakdown current and glows by thermal radiation
Current flows when light falls on it
pn-junction-016.explanation: When forward voltage is applied to an LED, electrons are injected from the n side and holes from the p side into the junction, and when they recombine they release energy corresponding to the band gap as light. Current flowing when light falls on the device is how a photodiode works.

pn-junction-017.question: Which is a characteristic of a PIN diode, which has a lightly doped i-layer between the p and n layers?
choices: It can amplify current
Its forward voltage is 0 V
The i-layer acts as a wide depletion layer, making it suitable for high breakdown voltage and for fast, sensitive photodetectors
pn-junction-017.explanation: In a PIN diode, the whole lightly doped i-layer acts as a depletion layer. Because the wide depletion layer can support high voltage, it is used for high-voltage diodes; and because the light-absorbing region is wide and the junction capacitance small, it is used for fast, sensitive photodetectors. It is also used as an RF switch.

pn-junction-018.question: Which is a characteristic of an avalanche photodiode (APD)?
choices: It emits strong light when current flows
It uses avalanche multiplication to amplify the photocurrent internally and can detect very weak light
It converts AC to DC
pn-junction-018.explanation: An APD is a photodiode biased with a large reverse voltage close to breakdown, so carriers generated by light are multiplied by avalanche multiplication and collected as a large current. Because it can detect very weak light with high sensitivity, it is used in optical communication receivers and LiDAR.

pn-junction-019.question: In the diode equation I = Is {exp(qV / nkT) − 1}, what current flows when a large reverse voltage is applied (within the range where no breakdown occurs)?
choices: It becomes infinite
It keeps increasing in proportion to exp(qV / nkT)
It stays nearly constant at about −Is (the reverse saturation current)
pn-junction-019.explanation: With a large reverse voltage (V a large negative value), exp(qV/nkT) is nearly 0, so I ≈ −Is. Only a tiny, nearly constant reverse saturation current flows. In real diodes, increasing the voltage further leads to breakdown.

pn-junction-020.question: What is the purpose of a diode (flyback diode) connected in parallel with an inductive load such as a relay coil?
choices: To amplify the coil current
To safely release the high back EMF generated when the switch is turned off and protect the driving device
To make the coil emit light
pn-junction-020.explanation: When current through a coil is cut off suddenly, the coil tries to keep the current flowing and generates a high back EMF that can destroy the driving transistor. A diode connected in reverse across the coil lets this current flow through it, preventing the high voltage.

pn-junction-021.question: In a forward-biased PN junction, which capacitance arises from the storage of injected minority carriers?
choices: Diffusion capacitance
Junction (depletion) capacitance
Wiring capacitance
pn-junction-021.explanation: Under forward bias, minority carriers are injected and stored on both sides of the junction, and their amount changes with voltage, so they act as a capacitance. This is the diffusion capacitance, which grows with forward current. Under reverse bias, the junction capacitance of the depletion layer dominates.

pn-junction-022.question: How does the depletion width of a one-sided abrupt junction depend on the reverse bias voltage V (when V is much larger than the built-in potential)?
choices: It is proportional to V
It is proportional to V squared
It is roughly proportional to the square root of V
pn-junction-022.explanation: The depletion width of a one-sided abrupt junction is W ∝ √(Vbi + V), so for large V it is roughly proportional to √V. The junction capacitance therefore decreases roughly as 1/√V. The lower the doping on the lightly doped side, the wider the depletion layer.

pn-junction-023.question: Why are termination structures such as guard rings placed at the edge (periphery) of a high-voltage PN junction?
choices: To make the junction emit light
To prevent the electric field from concentrating at the junction edge and causing breakdown at a lower voltage than designed
To increase the junction capacitance
pn-junction-023.explanation: Real junctions are finite, and their curved edges concentrate the electric field, so they break down at a lower voltage than the flat part. Termination structures such as guard rings and field plates relax the field at the edge so that the designed breakdown voltage is achieved. This is especially important in power devices.

pn-junction-024.question: In a simple voltage regulator using a Zener diode, what is the role of the resistor placed in series with the diode?
choices: To limit the current through the diode and take up the difference between input and output voltage
To amplify the signal
To convert AC to DC
pn-junction-024.explanation: A Zener diode keeps a nearly constant voltage in breakdown even as current changes, but without current limiting it would be destroyed by excess current. The series resistor limits the current and absorbs input voltage variations as a voltage drop, so the output voltage stays nearly constant.

pn-junction-025.question: Which diode, made from a PN junction very heavily doped on both sides, shows a negative-resistance region where current decreases as forward voltage increases?
choices: Schottky barrier diode
PIN diode
Tunnel diode (Esaki diode)
pn-junction-025.explanation: A tunnel diode is a PN junction doped so heavily on both sides that it is degenerate. Its depletion layer is very thin, so tunneling current flows at low forward voltages. As voltage increases, the tunneling current falls, creating a negative-resistance region used for high-frequency oscillators. It is also called the Esaki diode after its discoverer, Leo Esaki.

pn-junction-026.question: What is the typical open-circuit voltage of a single crystalline silicon solar cell?
choices: About 6 V
About 0.6–0.7 V
About 60 V
pn-junction-026.explanation: A single crystalline silicon solar cell has an open-circuit voltage of about 0.6–0.7 V. That is why practical solar modules connect many cells in series to obtain the required voltage.

pn-junction-027.question: Which value is closest to the theoretical maximum efficiency of a single-junction solar cell (the Shockley-Queisser limit)?
choices: About 100%
About 80%
About 33%
pn-junction-027.explanation: A single PN junction solar cell cannot absorb light with energy below the band gap, and the excess energy of higher-energy light is lost as heat. As a result, even with the optimal band gap, the theoretical efficiency limit is about 33%. Multi-junction solar cells and other approaches are being studied to exceed it.

pn-junction-028.question: How does the avalanche breakdown voltage generally change as temperature rises?
choices: It increases
It decreases
It does not change
pn-junction-028.explanation: As temperature rises, scattering by lattice vibrations increases, making it harder for carriers to gain enough energy for impact ionization, so the avalanche breakdown voltage increases (a positive temperature coefficient). Zener breakdown, by contrast, occurs at a lower voltage as temperature rises.

pn-junction-029.question: What is the phenomenon in which forward current through a PIN diode injects many carriers into the i-layer and greatly reduces its resistance?
choices: Early effect
Conductivity modulation
Hall effect
pn-junction-029.explanation: The lightly doped i-layer normally has high resistance, but under forward current, large numbers of electrons and holes are injected from the p and n layers and its resistance drops sharply. This is conductivity modulation, the mechanism that lets high-voltage diodes and IGBTs combine high breakdown voltage with low on-state voltage.

pn-junction-030.question: What can be evaluated by measuring the capacitance of a reverse-biased PN junction while varying the voltage (C-V measurement)?
choices: The color of emitted light
Only the carrier mobility
The doping concentration on the lightly doped side and its depth profile
pn-junction-030.explanation: Increasing reverse bias widens the depletion layer and reduces capacitance. How it changes depends on the doping at the edge of the depletion layer, so C-V measurements can determine the doping concentration on the lightly doped side and its depth profile.

pn-junction-031.question: Of the two terminals of a PN junction diode, what is the terminal on the p-type side called?
choices: Cathode
Anode
Gate
pn-junction-031.explanation: The terminal on the p-type side of a diode is called the anode, and the terminal on the n-type side is the cathode. When the anode is at a higher potential than the cathode, the diode is forward biased and current flows. In the circuit symbol, the triangle side is the anode and the bar side is the cathode.
choiceNotes: The cathode is the n-type side terminal.
Correct. The p-type side terminal is the anode.
A gate is the control terminal of a MOSFET or thyristor; a diode has none.

pn-junction-032.question: What is the property of a diode that lets current flow easily in one direction but hardly at all in the other called?
choices: Rectification
Amplification
The photoelectric effect
pn-junction-032.explanation: The property of conducting well in the forward direction and hardly at all in the reverse direction is called rectification. Rectifier circuits that convert AC to DC are built using this property.
choiceNotes: Correct. Conducting in only one direction is rectification.
Amplification makes small signals larger and is done by devices such as transistors.
The photoelectric effect is the emission of electrons or generation of carriers by light.

pn-junction-033.question: Which statement correctly describes the depletion layer of a PN junction in thermal equilibrium?
choices: Many majority carriers are gathered there
Electrons and holes are both present at high, equal densities
There are almost no carriers, and the charges of ionized impurities remain
pn-junction-033.explanation: Near the junction, electrons and holes diffuse and recombine, leaving a region with almost no carriers. This is the depletion layer: negatively charged acceptor ions remain on the p side and positively charged donor ions on the n side, creating the built-in electric field.
choiceNotes: The depletion layer is a region from which majority carriers have been swept out.
There are almost no carriers in the depletion layer.
Correct. Carriers are depleted, and the charges of fixed ions remain.

pn-junction-034.question: In which direction is a voltage regulator (Zener) diode normally used in a voltage regulator circuit?
choices: Reverse biased beyond its breakdown voltage
Forward biased
With no bias applied
pn-junction-034.explanation: A Zener diode uses the property that once the reverse voltage reaches the breakdown voltage, current flows sharply while the voltage stays almost constant even as the current changes. It is therefore used in reverse bias, with the cathode at a higher potential than the anode, operating in the breakdown region.
choiceNotes: Correct. The reverse breakdown region provides a constant voltage.
In forward bias it behaves like an ordinary diode, simply conducting at about 0.6 to 0.7 V.
Without bias, it does not regulate voltage.

pn-junction-035.question: When a sinusoidal AC signal is applied to a half-wave rectifier made of one diode and a resistor, what is the output?
choices: The AC signal passes through unchanged
The negative half-cycles are also flipped and output as positive
Only one half-cycle, either positive or negative, is output
pn-junction-035.explanation: In a half-wave rectifier, current flows only during the half-cycle in which the diode is forward biased, and the other half-cycle is blocked. The output therefore consists of only one half of each cycle. To use both halves, a full-wave rectifier such as a bridge rectifier is used.
choiceNotes: The diode blocks reverse current, so the AC does not pass unchanged.
Flipping the negative half-cycles is what a full-wave rectifier does.
Correct. Only one half-cycle is output.

pn-junction-036.question: When an LED is connected to a power supply to light it, what is the main purpose of a resistor in series with the LED?
choices: To limit the current through the LED to a suitable value
To change the LED's emission color
To raise the LED's reverse breakdown voltage
pn-junction-036.explanation: An LED is a diode whose current rises sharply above its forward voltage, so connecting it directly to a supply would let excessive current flow and destroy it. A series resistor limits the current; its value is (supply voltage − LED forward voltage) ÷ desired current.
choiceNotes: Correct. It limits the current to protect the LED.
The color is set by the semiconductor material, not the resistor.
A series resistor does not raise the reverse breakdown voltage.

pn-junction-037.question: What is the main purpose of placing a capacitor in parallel with the output of a rectifier?
choices: To reduce the ripple of the output voltage and make it closer to DC
To lower the forward voltage of the diode
To raise the frequency of the AC
pn-junction-037.explanation: The output of a rectifier alone is a pulsating voltage. A parallel capacitor charges when the voltage is high and discharges to support the voltage when it falls, reducing the ripple and giving an output close to DC. This is called a smoothing circuit.
choiceNotes: Correct. The capacitor's charging and discharging flattens the ripple.
A capacitor does not change the forward voltage of the diode.
A capacitor does not change the frequency.

pn-junction-038.question: How does the forward voltage of a silicon diode carrying a constant current change as the temperature rises?
choices: It rises at about 2 mV/°C
It does not change
It falls at about 2 mV/°C
pn-junction-038.explanation: The forward voltage of a silicon diode at constant current drops by about 2 mV for every 1 °C rise. The intrinsic carrier density increases with temperature, so less voltage is needed to pass the same current. This property is also used in temperature sensors.
choiceNotes: The forward voltage falls, not rises, as temperature increases.
The forward voltage has a clear temperature dependence.
Correct. Its temperature coefficient is about −2 mV/°C.

pn-junction-039.question: For an ideal diode (ideality factor n = 1) at room temperature, roughly how much must the forward voltage increase to raise the forward current tenfold?
choices: About 6 mV
About 60 mV
About 600 mV
pn-junction-039.explanation: The forward current is proportional to exp(qV/kT), so increasing the current tenfold requires increasing V by kT/q × ln 10 ≈ 26 mV × 2.3 ≈ 60 mV. This is the origin of the rule of thumb of about 60 mV per decade.
choiceNotes: About 6 mV only raises the current by a factor of about 1.3.
Correct. kT/q × ln 10 ≈ 60 mV.
About 600 mV would raise the current by a factor of about 10¹⁰.

pn-junction-040.question: Which expression gives the depletion (junction) capacitance C of a reverse-biased PN junction in terms of junction area A, depletion width W and semiconductor permittivity ε?
choices: C = εA / W
C = εW / A
C = ε / (A × W)
pn-junction-040.explanation: The depletion layer behaves like an insulating layer with charge stored on both sides, so it can be expressed like a parallel-plate capacitor as C = εA/W. Increasing the reverse bias widens W and reduces the capacitance.
choiceNotes: Correct. It has the same form as a parallel-plate capacitor.
A wider W means a smaller capacitance, so W belongs in the denominator.
A larger A means a larger capacitance, so A belongs in the numerator.

pn-junction-041.question: Why does no current flow externally in a PN junction in thermal equilibrium?
choices: Because carriers do not move at all in the depletion layer
Because the diffusion current and the drift current due to the built-in field cancel each other
Because all electrons and holes have recombined
pn-junction-041.explanation: In a PN junction in equilibrium, the diffusion current caused by the difference in carrier density balances the drift current flowing in the opposite direction due to the built-in field. The net current is zero for both electrons and holes, so no current flows externally.
choiceNotes: Carriers do move, but diffusion and drift balance so that the net flow is zero.
Correct. The diffusion and drift currents balance.
Not all carriers recombine; majority carriers remain in the neutral regions on both sides.

pn-junction-042.question: Which is the correct definition of the fill factor (FF) of a solar cell?
choices: Maximum power ÷ (open-circuit voltage × short-circuit current)
Short-circuit current ÷ open-circuit voltage
Output power ÷ incident light energy
pn-junction-042.explanation: The fill factor is the power at the maximum power point divided by the product of the open-circuit voltage and short-circuit current. It indicates how close the current-voltage curve is to a rectangle, and it decreases with losses such as a large series resistance. Conversion efficiency is the maximum power divided by the incident light power.
choiceNotes: Correct. FF = Pmax / (Voc × Isc).
Current divided by voltage is not the fill factor.
Output power divided by incident light power is the conversion efficiency.

pn-junction-043.question: Roughly what is the small-signal (dynamic) resistance of an ideal silicon diode carrying a forward current of 1 mA at room temperature? (kT/q ≈ 26 mV)
choices: About 2.6 Ω
About 260 Ω
About 26 Ω
pn-junction-043.explanation: The dynamic resistance of a diode is the reciprocal of the slope of its current-voltage curve, rd = nkT/(qI). With n = 1 and I = 1 mA, rd = 26 mV ÷ 1 mA = 26 Ω. The larger the current, the smaller the dynamic resistance.
choiceNotes: About 2.6 Ω is the value at a current of 10 mA.
About 260 Ω is the value at a current of 0.1 mA.
Correct. 26 mV ÷ 1 mA = 26 Ω.

pn-junction-044.question: How does the breakdown voltage of a PN junction generally change when the impurity concentration on one side is lowered?
choices: It becomes lower
It becomes higher
It does not depend on impurity concentration
pn-junction-044.explanation: With a lower impurity concentration, the depletion layer extends further at the same voltage and the field in the junction is weaker. A higher voltage is then needed to reach the critical field for avalanche breakdown, so the breakdown voltage rises. This is why high-voltage power devices use lightly doped drift layers.
choiceNotes: Heavier doping lowers the breakdown voltage; lighter doping raises it.
Correct. The depletion layer widens and the field weakens, so the breakdown voltage rises.
The breakdown voltage depends strongly on impurity concentration.

pn-junction-045.question: What is the main role of ESD protection diodes connected to the input/output pins of an IC?
choices: To amplify signals
To divert excessive voltages such as static discharge to the supply or ground and protect internal circuits
To increase pin capacitance and speed up signals
pn-junction-045.explanation: Electrostatic discharge (ESD) from people or equipment can reach thousands of volts. With diodes between the I/O pins and the supply and ground, the diodes conduct when an excessive voltage appears and divert the current, preventing damage to internal circuits such as gate oxides.
choiceNotes: ESD protection diodes do not amplify.
Correct. They divert excessive voltages to protect internal circuits.
Their capacitance actually slows signals, so it is designed to be small.

pn-junction-046.question: Zener diodes with a Zener voltage of about 5 to 6 V show little change in voltage with temperature. Why?
choices: Because no current flows through the diode at this voltage
Because tunneling (Zener) breakdown, with a negative temperature coefficient, and avalanche breakdown, with a positive one, occur to similar degrees and cancel
Because the band gap of silicon does not change with temperature
pn-junction-046.explanation: Diodes with low breakdown voltages (below about 5 V) break down mainly by tunneling (Zener breakdown), and their breakdown voltage falls as temperature rises. Higher-voltage ones break down mainly by avalanche, and their breakdown voltage rises with temperature. Around 5 to 6 V, the two effects work to similar degrees and the temperature coefficient is nearly zero.
choiceNotes: A Zener diode is used by passing current in its breakdown region.
Correct. Two breakdown mechanisms with opposite temperature coefficients cancel.
Silicon's band gap does change slightly with temperature.

pn-junction-047.question: What is a common way to make a metal-semiconductor contact ohmic (resistive)?
choices: Make the semiconductor surface at the contact lightly doped
Insert a thick oxide between the metal and semiconductor
Heavily dope the semiconductor surface at the contact so carriers can tunnel through the barrier easily
pn-junction-047.explanation: A Schottky barrier forms between a metal and a semiconductor, but heavily doping the semiconductor makes the barrier extremely thin, letting carriers tunnel through it. This gives a low-resistance contact regardless of current direction (an ohmic contact).
choiceNotes: Light doping makes the barrier thicker and tends to produce a Schottky contact.
A thick insulator makes current flow harder.
Correct. Heavy doping thins the barrier and allows tunneling current.

pn-junction-048.question: In the diode current expression I ∝ exp(qV / nkT), when is the ideality factor n close to 2?
choices: When minority carrier diffusion current in the neutral regions dominates
When recombination current in the depletion layer dominates
When tunneling current dominates
pn-junction-048.explanation: When minority carrier diffusion current dominates, n ≈ 1, but when recombination current through defect levels in the depletion layer dominates, n approaches 2. In silicon diodes, recombination current is noticeable at low currents, and n tends to be larger there.
choiceNotes: When diffusion current dominates, n ≈ 1.
Correct. Recombination current in the depletion layer gives n ≈ 2.
Tunneling current does not follow the temperature dependence of the form exp(qV/nkT).

pn-junction-049.question: When a reverse bias is applied to an abrupt PN junction, where is the electric field strongest?
choices: At the junction interface where p-type meets n-type
At the edges of the depletion layer
At the contacts with the electrodes
pn-junction-049.explanation: The field in the depletion layer is built up by integrating the charges of the ionized impurities; it is zero at the depletion layer edges and maximum at the metallurgical junction. Avalanche breakdown occurs when this maximum field reaches the critical field.
choiceNotes: Correct. The field peaks at the junction interface.
The field is zero at the edges of the depletion layer.
There is almost no field in the neutral regions near the electrodes.

pn-junction-050.question: Which correctly describes the depletion approximation used in analyzing PN junctions?
choices: Majority carriers are assumed to exist in the depletion layer at the same density as the impurities
The impurity concentrations on both sides of the junction are assumed to be equal
The depletion layer is assumed to contain no carriers at all, and the regions outside it are assumed to be charge-neutral
pn-junction-050.explanation: The depletion approximation assumes that the depletion layer contains no free carriers, only the charges of ionized impurities, and that the regions outside it are electrically neutral. This simplification with sharp boundaries allows the depletion width, field and capacitance to be obtained with simple formulas.
choiceNotes: The depletion approximation assumes almost no carriers in the depletion layer.
The doping can differ on the two sides; it is not assumed to be equal.
Correct. Zero carriers inside the depletion layer and neutrality outside.
